# File and policy checks

Everything reported about the files themselves rather than about a rule: YAML
that will not parse, a rules directory that cannot be read, and a policy file
configuring something it cannot configure.

All of these are fixed at `error`, and the reason is the same in each case:
they describe configuration that was not applied. A typo that silently drops a
setting is worse than one that fails, because the file reads as though it took
effect. There is nothing here for policy to soften, and a policy file cannot
soften the checks that police policy files.

## The file

<a id="yaml-syntax"></a>

### yaml/syntax

The file is not valid YAML.

The one failure that stops everything, because nothing after it can be read.
Every other check collects problems and carries on, so a single run reports as
much as it can rather than making a contributor fix one line at a time.

<a id="yaml-unknown-field"></a>

### yaml/unknown-field

A field nobody recognises.

Unknown fields are refused rather than ignored, because ignoring one means a
setting somebody wrote never takes effect and nothing says so. A misspelled
`sevrity:` would otherwise leave a check at its default while the file claims
it was raised.

```yaml
# before, and the rule keeps its default severity
checks:
  labels/required:
    sevrity: error

# after
checks:
  labels/required:
    severity: error
```

<a id="yaml-type"></a>

### yaml/type

A field holding the wrong shape, such as a list where a mapping belongs.

Reported with the line of the offending node, like every other finding, so the
fix is visible on the diff rather than in a stack trace.

<a id="ruleset-directory"></a>

### ruleset/directory

The rules directory, or a file inside it, could not be read.

An operational failure rather than a finding about anybody's rules, but it
blocks: a directory that could not be read has reported nothing about the
rules inside it, and carrying on would check fewer rules than the author
thinks and pass.

## The policy file

<a id="policy-unknown-check"></a>

### policy/unknown-check

A policy file configuring a check that does not exist.

Almost always a typo, and refusing it is the difference between a repository
where `rule/select-stars: error` is caught in review and one where it sits in
the file for a year looking like a control that is in place.

Every check the ruler can report is listed in the [index](index.md). A name
that is not on that page cannot be configured, because nothing would read it.

<a id="policy-fixed-check"></a>

### policy/fixed-check

A policy file configuring a correctness check.

Correctness checks have no severity to resolve: a rule that fails one cannot
do its job. Accepting the line silently would leave an operator believing they
had softened something that still blocks, which is worse than refusing it. The
list of which checks are fixed is in the [index](index.md).

If what you actually need is one cluster where a check is expected to fire,
that is an exemption on the source rather than a change in policy, and it
still cannot apply to a fixed check.

<a id="policy-severity"></a>

### policy/severity

A severity that is not `off`, `warn` or `error`.

`warning` is accepted as a spelling of `warn`. Anything else is refused rather
than guessed at, because the guess would decide whether a repository blocks on
a finding.

<a id="policy-check-limit"></a>

### policy/check-limit

A ceiling that is not written as `name:number`.

Ceilings ride the same `keys` list every other configurable check uses, so
they have to be readable as a name and a number. A key that does not parse is
not a ceiling, and reading it as the shipped default would leave an operator
believing they had set a limit that never applied.

```yaml
# before: neither of these is a ceiling
checks:
  rule/complexity:
    keys: [max-joins, max-subqueries:many]

# after
checks:
  rule/complexity:
    keys: [max-joins:4, max-subqueries:2]
```
